title: Standing up for rights
hook: Sikh groups defend the right to wear articles of faith at work, school and in the forces

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat, and your line was neighbors. Today, what happens when a neighbor is told they can't come in as they are.

A schoolboy in England is offered a place at a private school, on one condition: take off the turban and cut the hair, to match the uniform. His father refuses. The family takes the school to court, loses, appeals, and the case climbs all the way to the House of Lords, then the country's highest court. There the judges decide that Sikhs are protected under Britain's race relations law, and that the school's rule was unlawful discrimination. One boy, one turban, and a ruling that reached far beyond one school gate.
screen: `TAKE OFF THE TURBAN, OR NO PLACE.` → `THE FATHER REFUSES.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE LORDS.`

segments.voice: First, what's at stake. The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, asks initiated Sikhs to keep the five articles of faith, among them uncut hair and the kirpan, a small sword. For a Sikh who keeps them, they're not accessories to take off for work. So when a job, a school or an army says no, it becomes a question of rights. Second, the cases. The English case was Mandla against Dowell Lee. In Canada, a student named Gurbaj Singh Multani took his school board to the Supreme Court of Canada over wearing his kirpan, and the court ruled that a total ban was not justified. In the United States, Sikh soldiers and advocacy groups such as the Sikh Coalition pressed the army to let observant Sikhs serve with turbans and beards. Third, the wider reason. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life defending the freedom of Kashmiri Hindus to practice their own faith, not his. Sikhs remember him as standing up for someone else's right. Fourth, the line underneath. At Ang 141 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork to a Muslim or beef to a Hindu. The word there is hakk, what rightly belongs to someone, and some Sikhs read the line widely: a right isn't a favor, and taking it away is taking something that isn't yours. Some Sikh groups argue that a ruling won for a turban protects a headscarf, a kippah and a cross as well.
screen: `ARTICLES OF FAITH, NOT ACCESSORIES.` · `ENGLAND, CANADA, THE US ARMY.` · `GURU TEGH BAHADUR, FOR OTHERS.` · `ANG 141: ANOTHER'S RIGHT.` · then, large: `RIGHTS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose right is being quietly squeezed: someone talked over at work, someone told their name is too hard to say, someone asked to hide who they are to fit in. Feel your feet steady on the floor as you hold them in mind, and on each breath out wish them a fair hearing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.
Hakk. What rightly belongs to someone, the right Sikh groups have defended to wear articles of faith at work, at school and in the forces. Today's word.
Your line: rights for all. A right is something owed, never a favor. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikh advocacy groups help Sikhs who are told to remove a turban or kirpan at work, school or in the military, and often work alongside other faith groups on religious freedom.
